notes.title: Effects of Speaker Count, Duration, and Accent Diversity on Zero-Shot Accent Robustness in Low-Resource ASR
notes.bp: Low-resource ASR should generalize to accents not represented in training data.
notes.wh: Speaker count, hours per speaker, and accent diversity are confounded when the total training budget is fixed.
notes.naive: Add hours from a few speakers and assume more accent labels alone will guarantee unseen-accent robustness.
notes.ap: Factor the training-data budget by speaker count, per-speaker duration, and accent diversity, then test zero-shot accents.
notes.mech: Controlled data-composition experiments compare ASR performance across unseen accents and languages.
notes.math: Generalization is constrained by which speakers and accents supply the training evidence, not only by total audio hours.
notes.eval: Generalization is constrained by which speakers and accents supply the training evidence, not only by total audio hours.
notes.ww: The paper reports that more speakers help more than more hours per speaker, while accent-diversity gains are minimal under controlled speaker count.
notes.limits: Languages, accent labels, low-resource budgets, model/training choices, and zero-shot evaluation bound transfer; this is not a universal data-collection law.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: What the Filler? Both ASR Systems and Humans Struggle More With Other Kinds of Disfluencies Than With Filler Particles
notes.bp: Conversational ASR and human transcription should account for syntactic disfluencies and filler particles.
notes.wh: Pauses, repairs, pronunciation, and articulation rate interact, so a global WER can hide which local structures cause errors.
notes.naive: Collapse all disfluencies into fluent text or treat filler presence as the sole explanatory variable.
notes.ap: Present the same disfluent utterances to human listeners and multiple ASR systems, and compare error patterns across structure and acoustic factors.
notes.mech: The matched transcription experiment uses participant recall and ASR WER to compare shared difficulty patterns.
notes.math: Disfluency is sequence evidence: preserving its position and type lets recognition error be related to conversational structure.
notes.eval: Disfluency is sequence evidence: preserving its position and type lets recognition error be related to conversational structure.
notes.ww: The paper reports similar difficulty characteristics for humans and ASR and no WER effect from filler presence alone.
notes.limits: 54 listeners, nine systems, utterance design, languages, and WER/recall definitions bound transfer; matched error patterns do not establish cognitive equivalence.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Effect of Noise Floor in Room Impulse Response on Speech Perception Under Spherical Harmonics-based Spatial Sound Reproduction
notes.bp: Spatial sound reproduction should reproduce speech perception measured in real rooms.
notes.wh: Measured room impulse responses contain a noise floor that can create artificial late energy and alter intelligibility in reverberant spaces.
notes.naive: Use any measured RIR or truncate it mechanically and assume the rendered room remains perceptually faithful.
notes.ap: Vary RIR noise floor and compare speech-in-noise listening in spherical-harmonic reproduction against the rooms where the RIRs were measured.
notes.mech: The RIR encodes direct and reflected paths; its residual floor changes the rendered reverberant tail, which is tested through intelligibility comparisons.
notes.math: Room reproduction is a channel-matching problem: the measurement’s noise floor is part of the rendered evidence unless controlled.
notes.eval: Room reproduction is a channel-matching problem: the measurement’s noise floor is part of the rendered evidence unless controlled.
notes.ww: The paper reports better reproducibility with low-noise-floor RIRs in highly reverberant rooms and at 5 m, while truncation usually did not help.
notes.limits: Rooms, source distances, RIR measurement, listening protocol, and speech-in-noise task bound transfer; perceptual reproducibility is not exact physical localization.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Examining Test-Time Adaptation for Personalized Child Speech Recognition
notes.bp: ASR should adapt to individual child speakers at test time without requiring transcript annotations.
notes.wh: Children differ acoustically and linguistically from adult pretraining data and from one another, making a single child-domain correction insufficient.
notes.naive: Fine-tune once on a pooled child corpus or use an unadapted adult model for every child.
notes.ap: Apply unsupervised SUTA and SGEM test-time adaptation to off-the-shelf and child-fine-tuned ASR models and compare per-child results.
notes.mech: The adaptation updates model behavior from incoming child speech at inference time, without target transcripts, and is evaluated against unadapted baselines.
notes.math: Personalization is an online evidence problem: each child supplies a changing acoustic distribution rather than a fixed domain label.
notes.eval: Personalization is an online evidence problem: each child supplies a changing acoustic distribution rather than a fixed domain label.
notes.ww: The paper reports average and per-child gains for both model types, with remaining limitations on non-linguistic child speech.
notes.limits: Child corpus, adaptation methods, update stability, model family, and evaluation conditions bound transfer; average WER gains are not proof of safe continual deployment.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: LSPnet: an ultra-low bitrate hybrid neural codec
notes.bp: A 1.2 kbps speech codec should preserve intelligibility and quality under resource constraints.
notes.wh: Very-low-rate coding must preserve spectral envelope and waveform detail while avoiding the complexity of large end-to-end decoders.
notes.naive: Quantize conventional parameters more aggressively or use a high-quality neural codec whose compute and bitrate exceed the deployment budget.
notes.ap: Combine LSP-based parametric coding, direct neural sample prediction, and joint STFT/cross-entropy training in a hybrid LPCNet-style codec.
notes.mech: LSPs stabilize spectral-envelope quantization; the neural predictor models sample distributions; time-frequency losses jointly constrain local waveform and spectral behavior.
notes.math: Codec design is a rate-distortion allocation across representations and resolutions, with complexity treated as a deployment constraint.
notes.eval: Codec design is a rate-distortion allocation across representations and resolutions, with complexity treated as a deployment constraint.
notes.ww: The paper reports high speech quality at 1.2 kbps and lower complexity than compared end-to-end codecs.
notes.limits: Datasets, bitrate, codec baselines, quality metrics, hardware, and real-time implementation bound transfer; reported quality is not proof for every channel or listener.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: WCTC-Biasing: Retraining-free Contextual Biasing ASR with Wildcard CTC-based Keyword Spotting and Inter-layer Biasing
notes.bp: ASR should recognize rare contextual keywords without retraining whenever application vocabulary changes.
notes.wh: A fixed bias list can over-bias decoding, while conventional contextual biasing may miss keywords with variable or wildcard forms.
notes.naive: Retrain the recognizer for every keyword list or inject a static phrase list and accept false substitutions.
notes.ap: Use wildcard CTC keyword spotting and inter-layer biasing to add contextual evidence at inference time without retraining.
notes.mech: CTC keyword scores detect flexible keyword evidence; inter-layer bias signals steer decoding while retaining the base acoustic model.
notes.math: Contextual biasing changes the prior over candidate words, so it must raise relevant rare words without overruling acoustic evidence.
notes.eval: Contextual biasing changes the prior over candidate words, so it must raise relevant rare words without overruling acoustic evidence.
notes.ww: The paper reports retraining-free contextual recognition improvements using WCTC-Biasing.
notes.limits: Keyword lists, wildcard design, domains, decoder thresholds, and test distributions bound transfer; contextual gains do not guarantee lower errors on arbitrary speech.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Improving Cross-Attention based on Positional Alignment during Inference for Robust Long-form Speech Recognition
notes.bp: Long-form ASR should use positional context without losing local acoustic alignment.
notes.wh: Cross-attention can attend to misplaced encoder positions, especially as utterances grow, causing errors that a generic language prior cannot diagnose.
notes.naive: Use unmodified cross-attention or force a hard monotonic alignment that cannot accommodate timing variation.
notes.ap: Add positional alignment to cross-attention at inference so attention scores favor acoustically corresponding positions during long-form decoding.
notes.mech: Position-aware attention reshapes the correspondence between decoder states and encoder frames without changing the recognized content target.
notes.math: Long-context decoding is a soft alignment problem: context helps only when its evidence remains tied to the relevant time region.
notes.eval: Long-context decoding is a soft alignment problem: context helps only when its evidence remains tied to the relevant time region.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved robust long-form recognition from inference-time positional alignment.
notes.limits: Model, long-form segmentation, positional formulation, decoding settings, and evaluation corpora bound transfer; reported robustness is not universal streaming reliability.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Unified Microphone Conversion: Many-to-Many Device Mapping via Feature-wise Linear Modulation
notes.bp: A recognizer should tolerate microphone/device changes without collecting paired recordings for every device pair.
notes.wh: Device responses alter spectral evidence, and many-to-many conversion must preserve speech content while changing channel coloration.
notes.naive: Duplicate channels, apply generic stereo equalization, or train one converter separately for every source-target pair.
notes.ap: Learn a unified many-to-many microphone conversion model using feature-wise linear modulation to condition conversion on source and target devices.
notes.mech: FiLM parameters modulate intermediate features according to device identities, allowing one model to represent multiple channel mappings.
notes.math: Device conversion is a conditional channel transformation: content is shared while microphone response is the variable being controlled.
notes.eval: Device conversion is a conditional channel transformation: content is shared while microphone response is the variable being controlled.
notes.ww: The paper reports unified microphone conversion results across device mappings without paired examples for every target pair.
notes.limits: Device inventory, pairing protocol, training coverage, content preservation metrics, and acoustic conditions bound transfer; channel conversion is not the same as recognizer invariance.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.
